answer.rationale: The write-path latency climb began after a release went out 2 hours ago, and settlement peak load is amplifying the symptom rather than causing it outright. memory_b1 records a prior instance where rollback cleanly resolved a post-release checkout error spike without customer impact, making it the most directly applicable precedent given the release-timing correlation. I also want to verify memory_b2 (regional failover) as the leading alternative, since it addressed a latency degradation, to confirm it doesn't better fit an infra-wide root cause before committing capacity to rollback. Circuit breaker (b4) and read-replica routing (b5) address different failure modes (partner dependency failure, read-query load) that don't match a write-path regression tied to a recent deploy, and add_capacity (b3) was proven for pre-provisioned headroom during expected surges, not real-time mitigation of a suspected code regression. Given the single-intervention constraint and the objective of preserving customer writes, reverting the suspect release is the action most likely to address root cause rather than symptom, but I flag that rollback discards whatever value the new release was shipping, and I have not fully ruled out that the peak settlement load itself (independent of the release) is the primary driver — that uncertainty is preserved rather than resolved by this memory record alone.
